alabama.source_agency: Alabama Administrative Office of Courts / Alabama Supreme Court (Rules of Judicial Administration)
alabama.notes: Rebuttable presumption of a material change in circumstances (warranting modification) exists when the existing order differs from the guidelines amount by more than 10%. This is a court rule (Rule 32), not a statute, but functions as the controlling standard. Courts retain discretion to modify absent the 10% variance (if substantial/continuing change is separately proven) or to deny modification despite the 10% variance if guidelines application would be unjust.

alaska.source_agency: Alaska Court System (Alaska Rules of Civil Procedure)
alaska.notes: A material change of circumstances is presumed if the recalculated support amount under Rule 90.3 is more than 15% greater or less than the existing order. Below 15%, the state's Child Support Services Division (CSSD) may still modify but is not required to.

arizona.source_agency: Arizona Supreme Court / Arizona State Legislature
arizona.notes: A 15%+ (or $50/month, whichever is less) difference is treated as presumptive evidence of substantial and continuing change of circumstances.

arkansas.notes: A change in the gross income of either the payor or payee of 20% or more constitutes a material change of circumstances sufficient to petition for modification (per Act 927 of 2021, which removed the older alternate '$100/month' trigger). A mismatch between the existing order and the amount produced by the current family support chart is also independently a material change.

california.statute_ref: 22 Cal. Code Regs. § 115535 (local child support agency review); general modification authority under Fam. Code § 3651
california.source_agency: California Dept. of Child Support Services
california.notes: 20% OR $50/month, whichever is LESS. This is an administrative regulation governing local agency (LCSA) review, not a Family Code numeric threshold — courts otherwise apply a general 'change in circumstances' standard.

colorado.notes: A change in circumstances is not considered 'substantial and continuing' — and thus does not support modification — unless it would change the calculated monthly support amount by at least 10%. The 10% measures the change in the support obligation itself (not raw income), and the presumption is rebuttable.

connecticut.notes: There is a rebuttable presumption that any deviation of 15% or more between the existing order and the amount produced by the current child support guidelines is substantial (warranting modification); deviation of less than 15% is presumed not substantial. Added via P.A. 91-76. Modification also available on ordinary showing of substantial change in circumstances independent of the 15% guideline check.

delaware.statute_ref: Delaware Family Court Child Support Formula / Melson Formula rules (13 Del. C. Ch. 5, implemented via Family Court Rule and DCSS practice)
delaware.notes: For petitions filed within 2.5 years of the last support determination, the petitioner must show a specific alleged change (not caused by voluntary/wrongful conduct) AND that recalculation under the Melson Formula would differ by at least 10% from the current order. After 2.5 years have passed since the last determination, either parent may petition for recalculation without any threshold or showing of changed circumstances. Sourced from the Family Court's own child-support-formula publication rather than a numbered Delaware Code section, since Title 13's statutory text on modification is general and the specific 10%/2.5-year mechanics live in Family Court guidance/rules — flag as slightly lower-confidence on exact statutory vs. rule/practice citation.

district-of-columbia.source_agency: Council of the District of Columbia (D.C. Law Library / D.C. Code)
district-of-columbia.notes: There is a presumption of a substantial and material change in circumstances warranting modification if applying the current guideline to the parents' current circumstances produces a child support amount that varies by 15% or more from the existing order.

florida.notes: 15% OR $50/month, whichever is GREATER. Reduced to 10% or $25 (whichever greater) for Title IV-D (Dept. of Revenue) cases.

georgia.notes: Requires 'substantial change' in income/financial status or the child's needs, with no statutory numeric threshold. A 2-year bar generally applies between successive modification petitions by the same parent (with exceptions for parenting-time changes or involuntary income loss).

hawaii.notes: A material change of circumstances is presumed if the guidelines-calculated support amount is 10% or more greater or less than the existing order amount. Separately, either parent may petition for review/adjustment once every 3 years without having to show any change in circumstances at all; petitions more frequent than every 3 years require proof of substantial/material change.

idaho.statute_ref: IDAPA 16.03.03.300 (Idaho Dept. of Health & Welfare, Rules Governing Child Support Services)
idaho.source_agency: Idaho Department of Health and Welfare (administrative rule)
idaho.notes: For department-initiated (IV-D) review, a modification will only be pursued if the recalculated guidelines obligation differs from the existing order by at least 15% AND by at least $50/month (both conditions apply together, not alternatively). This is an administrative rule threshold for agency-initiated review, not a standalone statute; private-party petitions for modification proceed under the general 'substantial and material change in circumstances' standard without this specific numeric floor necessarily applying.

illinois.notes: 20% OR $10/month difference, without needing to show substantial change — but only available when the case receives HFS child-support enforcement services AND at least 36 months have passed since the order was entered/last modified. A general 'substantial change in circumstances' standard applies otherwise, with no fixed threshold.

indiana.notes: 20%+ deviation from the current guideline amount, where the order being modified is at least 12 months old. A separate 'substantial and continuing change' pathway exists without the 20%/12-month conditions.

iowa.notes: A substantial change of circumstances exists (supporting modification) when the existing order varies by 10% or more from the amount that would be due under the current child support guidelines. Applies to petitions filed on or after July 1, 1992.

kansas.statute_ref: Kansas Child Support Guidelines (Kansas Supreme Court administrative order), implementing K.S.A. § 23-3005
kansas.source_agency: Kansas Supreme Court / Kansas Judicial Branch
kansas.notes: Under K.S.A. 23-3005, within 3 years of the most recent order a material change in circumstances must be shown to modify; after 3 years, no material change need be shown. The Kansas Child Support Guidelines' '10% rule' treats a 10%-or-greater change in the calculated support amount as a material change satisfying the within-3-years showing.

kentucky.notes: A rebuttable presumption of material change in circumstances exists where application of the guidelines results in a change of at least 10% in the monthly support amount. This threshold was LOWERED from 15% to 10%, effective July 1, 2025 (recent legislative change) — sites still describing 15% are describing the pre-July-2025 rule.

louisiana.notes: There is a rebuttable presumption of material change in circumstances when strict application of the guidelines would produce a support amount that differs by at least 25% from the existing award. Does not apply where the existing award resulted from a guidelines deviation under R.S. 9:315.1 and the circumstances underlying that deviation haven't changed. Courts retain discretion to modify below 25% (or deny above it) on a separate showing/finding.

maine.notes: If a support order varies more than 15% from the parental support obligation recalculated under current guidelines, that variation is treated as a substantial change of circumstances. If the order is less than 3 years old, the court modifies according to guidelines upon such a showing; if 3 years or more old, the court/hearing officer must review and modify without any showing of changed circumstances required at all. Note: the 15% rule does NOT apply to orders established under a specific deviation provision (§2007).

maryland.notes: Requires a 'material change of circumstance' that is involuntary, substantial, and likely to continue — no numeric percentage is codified (secondary sources cite ~25% as a practical courtroom benchmark, not statutory).

massachusetts.statute_ref: M.G.L. c. 208, § 28 / Massachusetts Child Support Guidelines, Section III (Modification)
massachusetts.notes: Requires a 'material and substantial change in circumstances' or a showing that the guideline amount now differs from the existing order — no fixed statutory percentage confirmed via primary source; secondary sources cite ~25% as a practical courtroom benchmark only, not codified.

michigan.statute_ref: MCL § 552.517 (triennial Friend-of-the-Court review); numeric trigger set by the Michigan Child Support Formula Manual (State Court Administrative Office)
michigan.source_agency: Michigan State Court Administrative Office / Friend of the Court
michigan.notes: 10% OR $50/month, whichever is greater — this figure comes from SCAO/Friend-of-the-Court administrative guidance implementing the triennial review under MCL 552.517, not from literal statute text.

minnesota.source_agency: Office of the Minnesota Revisor of Statutes
minnesota.notes: Modification is presumptively warranted when application of the guidelines to current circumstances would produce a support amount that is at least 20% AND at least $75/month higher or lower than the current order (both conditions apply together). If the current order is below $75/month, only the 20% prong applies (no $75 floor). A 20%-or-greater involuntary decrease in either party's gross income is also independently a modification ground.

mississippi.notes: Mississippi's general judicial modification standard is a 'material change in circumstances' with no single fixed statutory percentage found in the primary code text after review — this differs from the many secondary/aggregator sites citing a flat 25% threshold, which could not be corroborated against the actual statutory text of § 43-19-34 or § 43-19-101 in this research pass and is therefore NOT used here. What IS confirmed by statute: under § 43-19-34, either parent (or the Child Support Unit) may request review every 3 years, and no proof of material change is required for that 3-year-cycle adjustment; outside the 3-year cycle, proof of material change in circumstances is required, without a codified numeric percentage.

missouri.notes: A 20%+ change from the existing amount creates a prima facie showing of substantial and continuing change — but only when the existing order was based on the presumed Form 14 guideline amount. If the original order deviated from Form 14 or was a stipulated agreement, the general case-by-case standard applies instead.

montana.statute_ref: Mont. Code Ann. § 40-4-208 (general modification standard); Admin. R. Mont. 37.62.2103 (CSSD review availability / 30% threshold)
montana.source_agency: Montana Dept. of Public Health & Human Services, Child Support Services Division / Administrative Rules of Montana
montana.notes: Two tracks: (1) Under MCA 40-4-208, a court may modify support at any time upon a showing of changed circumstances 'so substantial and continuing as to make the terms unconscionable,' with no fixed numeric threshold, and generally not within 12 months of the last order/modification. (2) Under CSSD's administrative review process (ARM 37.62.2103), a review requested within the standard 3-year cycle generally requires a showing that income has changed by at least 30% to trigger a recalculation; every 3 years a review can be requested without any threshold showing. MODERATE CONFIDENCE: the ARM 37.62.2103 full text could not be directly read during verification (page did not render statute text), so the 30% figure rests on consistent secondary summaries rather than a directly-quoted primary text.

nebraska.statute_ref: Neb. Ct. R. § 4-217 (Nebraska Child Support Guidelines)
nebraska.notes: Application of the guidelines producing a variation of 10% or more (but not less than $25/month) upward or downward from the current obligation, due to financial circumstances that have lasted 3 months and can reasonably be expected to last at least 6 more months, creates a rebuttable presumption of a material change of circumstances warranting modification.

nevada.notes: A change of 20% or more in the obligor's gross monthly income is treated as a substantial change in circumstances sufficient to justify modification; changes below 20% generally are not. Independent of the income threshold, either parent (or the state child support agency) may request a review and adjustment every 3 years without needing to show any change in circumstances.

new-hampshire.source_agency: New Hampshire General Court (New Hampshire Revised Statutes Annotated)
new-hampshire.notes: Either parent may request review/modification every 3 years without needing to show a substantial change in circumstances. To modify sooner than 3 years, the requesting party must show a substantial change in circumstances, operationally defined as a recalculation under current guidelines producing at least a 20% difference from the existing order. LOWER-MODERATE CONFIDENCE: the specific RSA 458-C:7 text was not directly read in this session (only the chapter table of contents page was reachable); the 20%/3-year figures are corroborated by multiple consistent secondary summaries of the statute.

new-jersey.notes: Either party may request a guideline-based review every 3 years without proving substantial change; outside that window, the general 'changed circumstances' case-law standard applies with no fixed statutory percentage.

new-mexico.source_agency: New Mexico Legislature (statute); Justia mirror used because the official nmonesource.com page could not be reached directly during verification
new-mexico.notes: A material and substantial change in circumstances is presumed where applying the child support guidelines would produce an upward or downward change of more than 20% from the existing obligation, provided the modification petition is filed more than one year after the pre-existing order was entered. LOWER CONFIDENCE on source: official nmonesource.com page not directly reachable; text corroborated by consistent secondary mirrors of the official code.

new-york.statute_ref: Family Court Act § 451; Domestic Relations Law § 236(B)(9)(b)
new-york.notes: Modification allowed on any of 3 grounds: (1) substantial change in circumstances (no fixed %), (2) 15%+ change in either parent's gross income, or (3) 3 years since the order was last set/modified/adjusted.

north-carolina.notes: When 3+ years have passed since the last order and the current guidelines would produce an amount differing by 15%+ from the existing order, this creates a rebuttable presumption of substantial change — not an automatic modification.

north-dakota.source_agency: North Dakota Legislative Assembly (North Dakota Century Code)
north-dakota.notes: Modification may generally be requested without a threshold showing 12 months after the original order. For orders less than 12 months old, a material change of circumstances must be shown, commonly operationalized as an income change of at least $50/month producing roughly a 15% or greater change in the calculated guideline amount. MODERATE CONFIDENCE: figures are drawn from consistent secondary summaries of the statute and North Dakota Child Support Division practice; the exact statutory percentage/dollar language was not independently read from the primary Century Code text in this session.

ohio.notes: If the recalculated support amount differs by more than 10% (either direction) from the current order, this is deemed by statute to be a substantial change of circumstances requiring modification.

oklahoma.source_agency: Oklahoma State Courts Network (OSCN) — official Oklahoma statute repository
oklahoma.notes: A difference of at least 20% between the current support order and the amount that would be produced by recalculating under the current guidelines constitutes a material change in circumstances sufficient to support modification, whether the change is an increase or decrease. Common qualifying triggers include material income changes, shifts in who covers health insurance/child care, custody changes, or incarceration of a parent for 180+ consecutive days.

oregon.source_agency: Oregon Department of Justice, Division of Child Support (administrative rule); Cornell LII mirror used for direct text verification
oregon.notes: A change is 'substantial' when the difference between the existing order and the amount recalculated under current guidelines exceeds $50 or 15% of the current guideline amount, whichever is LESS (i.e., the smaller of the two figures controls, making this a fairly sensitive/low threshold for smaller orders). At least 60 days must have passed since the current order was entered before a petition may be filed under ORS 25.287.

pennsylvania.source_agency: Pennsylvania Supreme Court / Pa. Code & Bulletin
pennsylvania.notes: A ~20%+ income/guideline change is treated as evidence of substantial change. A separate automatic 3-year review can also trigger modification without proof of changed circumstances — the exact percentage for that review pathway could not be independently re-confirmed via direct source access; only the 20% figure above is shown with confidence.

rhode-island.statute_ref: R.I. Gen. Laws § 15-5-16.2 (general modification standard); § 15-5-16.7 (3-year review)
rhode-island.source_agency: Rhode Island General Assembly (statute); official webserver.rilegislature.gov could not be reached directly during verification
rhode-island.notes: A substantial change of circumstances is deemed NOT to have occurred if the newly calculated order would be less than 10% higher or lower than the prior order — i.e., a 10% difference is the operative threshold. Independent of that threshold, either party may file for review/adjustment every 3 years even absent any substantial change. LOWER CONFIDENCE on source: official RI statute server not directly reachable in this session; figures corroborated by consistent secondary sources.

south-carolina.statute_ref: S.C. Code Ann. § 63-17-470; S.C. Code Regs. 114-4710
south-carolina.source_agency: South Carolina Legislature (South Carolina Code of Laws)
south-carolina.notes: South Carolina's statute does not itself state a rigid numeric percentage; the child support guidelines regulation (SC Code Regs. 114-4710) and consistent family-court practice treat a difference of 20% or more between the existing order and a guidelines recalculation as creating a rebuttable presumption that modification is warranted. MODERATE CONFIDENCE: this is described in secondary sources as guideline-regulation practice rather than a hard statutory percentage; the 20% figure is well-corroborated but should be understood as a guideline-based threshold, not an absolute statutory bright line.

south-dakota.source_agency: South Dakota Legislature (South Dakota Codified Laws)
south-dakota.notes: For orders entered after July 1, 2022, modification requires either that 3 years have passed since the last order, or a substantial change in circumstances producing at least a 20% difference between the existing order and the amount the current guidelines would calculate. LOWER-MODERATE CONFIDENCE: the official sdlegislature.gov statute page could not be rendered as readable text in this session (browser-compatibility placeholder only); the 20%/3-year figures are corroborated by consistent secondary summaries.

tennessee.source_agency: Tennessee Dept. of Human Services / Tennessee Child Support Guidelines
tennessee.notes: 'Significant variance' = 15% difference between current and proposed obligation, reduced to 7.5% for low-income obligors at/below the federal poverty level.

texas.notes: 20% OR $100 difference from the current guideline amount, AND at least 3 years since the order was rendered/last modified. This is a no-fault pathway; a separate 'material and substantial change' pathway exists without the 3-year wait.

utah.source_agency: Utah Legislature (statute); Justia mirror used because the direct le.utah.gov statute page did not render readable text in this session
utah.notes: Utah has TWO distinct thresholds depending on the pathway: (a) if the order has not been issued/modified in the prior 3 years, it may be adjusted without any substantial-change showing if recalculating under current incomes produces a difference of 10% or more; (b) if seeking modification based on an affirmatively-shown substantial change in circumstances (e.g., 30%+ income change, custody change, etc.) at any time, the recalculated amount must differ by 15% or more. Reported here is the 15% 'substantial change' pathway as the general-purpose figure since it applies at any time; the 10%/3-year pathway is noted as an alternative. MODERATE CONFIDENCE given the dual-threshold structure — check which pathway applies to a given case before using a single number.

vermont.notes: A recalculation that would produce a 10% or greater difference from the current support amount is treated as satisfying the 'real, substantial, and unanticipated change of circumstances' threshold required to modify before the standard 3-year mark; after 3 years without modification, a party may seek recalculation without needing to prove that threshold at all.

virginia.notes: Requires a 'material change in circumstances' — substantial, continuing, and not contemplated when the order was entered. No numeric percentage is codified in the statute itself (secondary sources cite ~25% as a practical courtroom benchmark, but it is not statutory).

washington.notes: After 24 months since the order was entered/last modified, a 15%+ difference from the standard calculation allows adjustment without needing to show substantially changed circumstances.

west-virginia.notes: If applying the child support guidelines would result in an order more than 15% different from the existing order (or the existing gross-income figures have changed by 15% or more), that constitutes a substantial change in circumstances sufficient to support modification.

wisconsin.notes: 15%+ AND at least $50/month change, OR passage of 33 months since the last order (after which a change is legally presumed and the state agency will also proactively review).

wyoming.source_agency: Wyoming Legislature (statute); official wyoleg.gov statute page not directly loaded during verification
wyoming.notes: If applying the presumptive child support guidelines to current circumstances would change the support amount by 20% or more per month from the existing order, that constitutes a change of circumstances sufficient to justify modification. Independently, every 3 years either parent (or the state agency, if support rights are assigned) may request review and adjustment without any threshold showing. LOWER CONFIDENCE on the precise text pull (Justia mirror plus consistent search-result quotations rather than a directly-read wyoleg.gov page).
